scenes.title: The Bloop
scenes.text: In 1997, something in the Pacific Ocean made a sound so loud, it was picked up by sensors more than five thousand kilometres apart.

scenes.title: Listening for submarines
scenes.text: The underwater microphones were built to listen for submarines. They had never heard anything like this.

scenes.title: The real recording
scenes.text: It rose fast and was far too powerful for any known animal. Listen.

scenes.title: A sea monster?
scenes.text: Many people believed it came from a giant, unknown creature in the deep.

scenes.title: NOAA's answer
scenes.text: Years later, scientists gave their answer: an icequake. A huge iceberg cracking and breaking away from Antarctica.

scenes.title: Would you go down there?
scenes.text: But for years, nobody knew what made it. Would you go down and look?

scenes.title: The Taos Hum
scenes.text: In Taos, a small desert town in New Mexico, some people hear a sound that others cannot hear.

scenes.title: A distant engine
scenes.text: A low, steady rumble, like a diesel engine idling far away. Day and night.

scenes.title: Who hears it?
scenes.text: In a survey in the 1990s, about two percent of the people living there said they could hear it.

scenes.title: Scientists came
scenes.text: Scientists came with sensitive microphones and instruments. They could not find where it comes from.

scenes.title: Can you hear it?
scenes.text: The ground, power lines, or something inside the ears of the people who hear it? Nobody knows. Would you want to hear it?

scenes.title: The Wow! Signal
scenes.text: On August fifteenth, 1977, a radio telescope in Ohio caught a signal from deep space.

scenes.title: The hydrogen line
scenes.text: It was strong and narrow, right next to the radio frequency of hydrogen, where scientists thought an alien message might be sent.

scenes.title: "Wow!"
scenes.text: Astronomer Jerry Ehman circled it on the printout and wrote one word: Wow!

scenes.title: 72 seconds
scenes.text: It lasted seventy two seconds, and came from the direction of the constellation Sagittarius.

scenes.title: It never came back
scenes.text: Astronomers have searched that spot for decades. It has never come back. Was it a message?

scenes.title: The Voynich Manuscript
scenes.text: This book is about six hundred years old, and nobody on Earth can read it.

scenes.title: Early 1400s
scenes.text: Carbon dating puts its pages in the early fourteen hundreds.

scenes.title: An unknown alphabet
scenes.text: It is written in an alphabet that appears nowhere else in the world.

scenes.title: Plants that don't exist
scenes.text: Its pages are full of plants nobody can identify, star charts, and strange drawings of bathing women.

scenes.title: Still unbroken
scenes.text: Codebreakers, linguists and even computers have tried. No one has cracked it.

scenes.title: Could you read it?
scenes.text: Today it is kept at Yale University. Do you think anyone will ever read it?

scenes.title: Never coming back
scenes.text: In 1977, NASA launched two spacecraft that will never come home: Voyager 1 and Voyager 2.

scenes.title: The grand tour
scenes.text: Together they flew past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, sending back the first close-up pictures of these worlds.

scenes.title: The Pale Blue Dot
scenes.text: In 1990, Voyager 1 turned around and photographed Earth from six billion kilometres away. A tiny blue dot.

scenes.title: Interstellar space
scenes.text: Today, both Voyagers have left the Sun's bubble and are in interstellar space, the farthest human-made objects ever.

scenes.title: A message for aliens
scenes.text: Each one carries a golden record with sounds and pictures of Earth, in case anyone ever finds it.

scenes.title: New Horizons
scenes.text: In 2015, a newer probe, New Horizons, gave us our first close look at Pluto, with its giant heart-shaped glacier.

scenes.title: Arrokoth
scenes.text: Then it flew past Arrokoth, the most distant object ever explored up close, and kept going.

scenes.title: Into the dark
scenes.text: None of them will ever return. When their power runs out, they will drift silently between the stars for millions of years.

scenes.title: Lost in the woods?
scenes.text: Lost in the woods, with wet wood and no lighter? Look for one thing: pine resin.

scenes.title: Pine resin
scenes.text: It's the sticky, golden sap that pine trees push out to seal their wounds. And it is full of flammable oils.

scenes.title: Fire starter
scenes.text: A small lump of resin catches a spark easily and burns hot for minutes, even when everything around it is damp.

scenes.title: Fatwood
scenes.text: Look for old pine stumps. Wood soaked with resin, called fatwood, smells like turpentine and lights almost instantly.

scenes.title: A torch
scenes.text: Smear resin on the end of a stick with dry bark, and you have a torch that burns for a long time.

scenes.title: Natural glue
scenes.text: Melt it, mix in fine charcoal, and it becomes a strong glue. People have used it to fix tools for thousands of years.

scenes.title: Waterproofing
scenes.text: It also seals cracks in containers and makes seams waterproof.

scenes.title: Take only a little
scenes.text: Only collect resin that has already leaked out, never cut the tree. Did you know this trick?

scenes.title: Same size, different power
scenes.text: These two engines are both two litres, with four cylinders. One makes about one hundred fifty horsepower. The other makes four hundred twenty one. How?

scenes.title: It's all about air
scenes.text: An engine is basically an air pump. The more air and fuel it can burn every second, the more power it makes.

scenes.title: Turbochargers
scenes.text: A turbocharger uses hot exhaust gas to spin a fan that squeezes extra air into the cylinders. More air, bigger explosion.

scenes.title: Revs
scenes.text: Power is force times speed. An engine that can safely spin faster makes more power from the same size.

scenes.title: Stronger parts
scenes.text: High power engines use forged pistons, stronger rods, better cooling and smarter computers, so they don't melt under the pressure.

scenes.title: The price
scenes.text: That's why the powerful one costs more, uses more fuel and needs more care. Which one would you choose?

scenes.title: A pyramid under the sea?
scenes.text: In 1986, a diver off the tiny Japanese island of Yonaguni found something strange on the sea floor.

scenes.title: The Yonaguni Monument
scenes.text: Giant stone terraces, flat platforms and sharp right angles, like steps, about twenty five metres under the water.

scenes.title: Lost civilization?
scenes.text: A Japanese geologist believed it was carved by people over ten thousand years ago, when this land was still above the sea.

scenes.title: Or nature?
scenes.text: Most scientists disagree. This sandstone naturally cracks along straight lines, which can create step-like shapes.

scenes.title: You decide
scenes.text: Natural rock, or the ruins of a lost world? What do you think?

scenes.title: How to add engine oil
scenes.text: Here's how to check and add engine oil, the right way, in under a minute.

scenes.title: 1. Park & wait
scenes.text: Park on level ground, turn the engine off, and wait about ten minutes. The oil drains back down, and the hot parts cool off.

scenes.title: 2. Find the dipstick
scenes.text: Open the hood and find the dipstick. It usually has a yellow or orange handle.

scenes.title: 3. Wipe & read
scenes.text: Pull it out, wipe it clean, push it all the way back in, then pull it out again. The oil should be between the two marks.

scenes.title: 4. Open the oil cap
scenes.text: If it's low, open the cap with the oil can symbol on top of the engine.

scenes.title: 5. Add a little at a time
scenes.text: Use the oil type from your owner's manual. Pour in a little, wait a minute, and check again. Never overfill.

scenes.title: Done
scenes.text: Close the cap tightly, and you're done. Check it once a month. Follow for more simple car tips.

scenes.title: The Doomsday Vault
scenes.text: Inside an Arctic mountain, there's a vault built to survive the end of the world.

scenes.title: Svalbard, Norway
scenes.text: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault sits on a Norwegian island, about 1,300 kilometres from the North Pole.

scenes.title: Into the rock
scenes.text: A tunnel runs over 100 metres into the rock, to chambers kept at minus 18 degrees.

scenes.title: The treasure
scenes.text: The treasure inside? Seeds. Over 1.3 million samples of the world's crops.

scenes.title: Built to last
scenes.text: Even if the power fails, the permafrost should keep them frozen.

scenes.title: The first withdrawal
scenes.text: In 2015, war in Syria cut scientists off from their gene bank near Aleppo. So they withdrew their backup seeds, and grew them again.

scenes.title: One seed at a time
scenes.text: The doomsday vault isn't just waiting for doomsday. It's already saving our crops.

scenes.title: The forbidden island
scenes.text: There is an island you are not allowed to visit. And its people want it that way.

scenes.title: North Sentinel Island
scenes.text: North Sentinel Island, in India's Andaman Islands: thick forest, ringed by coral reef.

scenes.title: The Sentinelese
scenes.text: It is home to the Sentinelese, one of the last uncontacted peoples on Earth.

scenes.title: A protected reserve
scenes.text: India protects it as a tribal reserve. Even sailing close is illegal.

scenes.title: After the tsunami
scenes.text: After the 2004 tsunami, a helicopter flew over to check on them. A man on the beach shot arrows at it.

scenes.title: Keep out
scenes.text: Outsiders who landed have been killed, most recently an American missionary in 2018.

scenes.title: Why stay away?
scenes.text: And contact could be deadly for them too. They may have no immunity to our diseases.

scenes.title: Eyes on, hands off
scenes.text: So the rule is simple: watch from afar, and leave them in peace.

scenes.title: Russia's secret mountain
scenes.text: In Russia's Ural Mountains, there's a mountain the United States spent years asking about.

scenes.title: Mount Yamantau
scenes.bigSub: highest peak of the Southern Urals
scenes.text: Mount Yamantau. At 1,640 metres, it's the highest peak in the Southern Urals.

scenes.title: A closed town
scenes.text: At its foot lies Mezhgorye, a closed military town that outsiders can't simply visit.

scenes.title: Inside the mountain
scenes.text: Since Soviet times, a huge underground complex has reportedly been built inside the mountain.

scenes.title: Changing answers
scenes.text: Asked what it was, Russian officials gave different answers. A mine. A store for treasures. A food warehouse. A bunker for leaders.

scenes.title: Washington asks
scenes.text: In 1997, the U.S. Congress urged Russia to explain it, and to allow an inspection.

scenes.title: Still a secret
scenes.text: Many analysts suspect a nuclear war bunker. But its purpose has never been confirmed.

scenes.title: Snake Island
scenes.text: Off the coast of Brazil lies an island you are not allowed to land on.

scenes.title: Ilha da Queimada Grande
scenes.text: Ilha da Queimada Grande, off São Paulo. Better known as Snake Island.

scenes.title: The golden lancehead
scenes.text: It is the only home on Earth of the golden lancehead, a highly venomous pit viper.

scenes.title: How many?
scenes.text: Scientists estimate a few thousand live here, on less than half a square kilometre.

scenes.title: Hunting in the trees
scenes.text: Cut off by rising seas long ago, with no prey on the ground, the snakes learned to hunt birds.

scenes.title: The lighthouse
scenes.text: A lighthouse has stood here since 1909. Legend says snakes killed its keeper's family, but there is no proof.

scenes.title: Who can land?
scenes.text: Today the light is automatic, and only the Navy and approved scientists may land.

scenes.title: Critically endangered
scenes.text: The ban protects the snakes too. They are critically endangered.

scenes.title: A 2,000-year-old computer
scenes.text: This lump of bronze came from a Greek shipwreck. Inside are gears, over two thousand years old.

scenes.title: The shipwreck
scenes.text: Divers found it in 1901, in a wreck off Antikythera that sank around 60 BC.

scenes.title: Hidden gears
scenes.text: Today it survives in 82 fragments, with 30 bronze gears.

scenes.title: A pocket cosmos
scenes.text: Turn a handle, and it showed the Sun, the Moon and its phases, and likely the planets.

scenes.title: Predicting the sky
scenes.bigSub: eclipse cycle on the back dial
scenes.text: It predicted eclipses, and even tracked the four-year Olympic cycle.

scenes.title: X-ray secrets
scenes.text: In 2005, X-ray scans revealed hidden gears and thousands of tiny inscriptions.

scenes.title: Rebuilding it
scenes.bigSub: UCL's new model of the front
scenes.text: In 2021, a UCL team rebuilt its lost front as a model of the cosmos.

scenes.title: Who built it?
scenes.text: Nothing this complex returns for a thousand years. Its maker is still a mystery.

scenes.title: The biggest stone of antiquity
scenes.text: See the tiny person? These are the biggest stone blocks known from the ancient world, and they never left the quarry.

scenes.title: Baalbek, Lebanon
scenes.text: This is Baalbek, Lebanon, and its giant Roman Temple of Jupiter.

scenes.title: Giant columns
scenes.text: Six columns still stand, each about twenty metres tall.

scenes.title: The trilithon
scenes.text: In its base: the trilithon, three blocks of about eight hundred tonnes each.

scenes.title: Stone of the Pregnant Woman
scenes.text: In the quarry lies the Stone of the Pregnant Woman: about a thousand tonnes, never moved.

scenes.title: An even bigger one
scenes.text: In 2014, archaeologists found a bigger one beside it: about sixteen hundred and fifty tonnes.

scenes.title: How did they do it?
scenes.text: Most archaeologists credit Roman engineers, with ramps, rollers and capstans, from a quarry just uphill.

scenes.title: Still debated
scenes.text: But exactly how the trilithon was lifted is still debated.

scenes.title: The last word
scenes.text: In 1947, a plane over the Andes sent one last word in Morse code. Stendec. Then it vanished.

scenes.title: Star Dust
scenes.text: Star Dust, an Avro Lancastrian with eleven people aboard, flying from Buenos Aires to Santiago.

scenes.title: The final message
scenes.text: Its final message ended with Stendec. No one has ever explained that word.

scenes.title: Vanished
scenes.text: Search teams found nothing. Rumours spread of sabotage, and even UFOs.

scenes.title: Mount Tupungato
scenes.text: In 1998, climbers on Mount Tupungato found its wreckage, coming out of a glacier.

scenes.title: The jet stream
scenes.text: Investigators concluded a powerful jet stream headwind had slowed the plane, so the crew descended too early, into the mountain.

scenes.title: Still a mystery
scenes.text: The glacier hid Star Dust for over fifty years. But Stendec is still a mystery.

scenes.title: A secret metro?
scenes.text: Under Moscow, there may be a second, secret metro.

scenes.title: Metro-2
scenes.text: It's called Metro-2. Reportedly, deep tunnels linking the Kremlin to government bunkers.

scenes.title: Started under Stalin?
scenes.text: The story says it was started under Stalin, and given the code name D-6.

scenes.title: A US report
scenes.text: A US Defense Department report later described it, with a diagram of the possible lines.

scenes.title: Where does it go?
scenes.text: One line is said to run toward Moscow State University.

scenes.title: Real bunkers
scenes.text: Real Cold War bunkers do exist here. Bunker 42 is now a museum.

scenes.title: Officially?
scenes.text: But Metro-2 itself? Officials have never confirmed it exists. And never clearly denied it.

scenes.title: Right below you
scenes.text: So next time you ride the Moscow metro, there might be another one right below you.

scenes.title: They never came back
scenes.text: In 1945, five U.S. Navy bombers left Florida on a training flight. They never came back.

scenes.title: Flight 19
scenes.text: Flight 19. Five TBM Avengers and fourteen men, led by Lieutenant Charles Taylor.

scenes.title: Lost
scenes.text: Taylor said his compasses had failed, and thought they were over the Florida Keys. Night fell, and fuel ran low.

scenes.title: The rescue plane
scenes.text: A Mariner flying boat with thirteen men went out to search. It vanished too.

scenes.title: Flying gas tanks
scenes.text: A ship saw a burst of flame in the sky. Mariners were nicknamed flying gas tanks.

scenes.title: A legend is born
scenes.text: Twenty seven men, gone in one day. And the legend of the Bermuda Triangle grew.

scenes.title: The twist
scenes.text: But here's the twist: the Coast Guard and insurers like Lloyd's say it's no more dangerous than any other busy stretch of sea.

scenes.title: Behind the wall
scenes.text: In 1963, a man in Türkiye knocked through a wall in his house, and found a passage.

scenes.title: Cappadocia, Türkiye
scenes.text: It led to a whole city carved into the rock beneath Derinkuyu, in Cappadocia.

scenes.title: How deep?
scenes.text: It reaches about eighty five metres down, with as many as eighteen levels by some counts.

scenes.title: A city for thousands
scenes.text: It may have sheltered up to twenty thousand people, along with their animals and food.

scenes.title: Life underground
scenes.text: There were stables, wine presses, wells, chapels, and air shafts reaching the surface.

scenes.title: Stone doors
scenes.text: Huge rolling stone doors could seal each level from the inside.

scenes.title: Why build it?
scenes.text: It was greatly expanded in Byzantine times, as a refuge from raids.

scenes.title: Look behind it
scenes.text: Today, part of it is open to visitors. So if you ever knock down a wall, look behind it.

scenes.title: The lighthouse mystery
scenes.text: In December 1900, three lighthouse keepers vanished from a remote Scottish island.

scenes.title: The Flannan Isles
scenes.text: Eilean Mòr, far out in the Atlantic. Just seabirds, cliffs and a lighthouse.

scenes.title: The light goes out
scenes.text: On the fifteenth of December, a passing steamer noticed the light was not shining.

scenes.title: No one waiting
scenes.text: Storms delayed the relief ship until Boxing Day. No one came down to meet it.

scenes.title: Gone
scenes.text: All three men were gone. One set of oilskins was still hanging inside.

scenes.title: Legend vs. record
scenes.text: Later tales added an untouched meal, a fallen chair and eerie log entries. None of that is in the official report.

scenes.title: The likely answer
scenes.text: Storm damage high above the west landing suggested a huge wave swept them away.

scenes.title: Never found
scenes.text: Their bodies were never found. The sea kept its secret.

scenes.title: The ghost ship
scenes.text: In December 1872, a ship was found adrift in the Atlantic, with no one aboard.

scenes.title: The Mary Celeste
scenes.text: She was the Mary Celeste, bound from New York to Genoa with barrels of alcohol.

scenes.title: Found adrift
scenes.text: Another ship, the Dei Gratia, found her about four hundred miles east of the Azores.

scenes.title: What was left
scenes.text: Six months of food and water were still aboard. But the lifeboat was gone.

scenes.title: Ten people
scenes.text: Captain Briggs, his wife, their little daughter and seven crew were never seen again.

scenes.title: The inquiry
scenes.text: An inquiry in Gibraltar found no sign of violence.

scenes.title: Fiction becomes legend
scenes.text: In 1884, Arthur Conan Doyle wrote a story about it, and its invented details became legend.

scenes.title: What happened?
scenes.text: One theory: fearing the alcohol might explode, they fled in the lifeboat.

scenes.title: Then vs Now
scenes.text: Then versus now. One ordinary day in America, in 1900.

scenes.title: Dawn deliveries
scenes.text: At dawn, the milkman and the iceman arrive by horse and wagon. There's no fridge.

scenes.title: No electricity
scenes.text: Fewer than one in twenty homes have electricity. You read by kerosene lamp.

scenes.title: The bathroom? Outside
scenes.text: The toilet? Usually an outhouse in the yard.

scenes.title: Work
scenes.text: The average worker puts in nearly sixty hours a week, often over six days.

scenes.title: A shorter life
scenes.text: A baby born in the US in 1900 could expect to live about forty seven years. Today, it's nearly eighty.

scenes.title: Dusk
scenes.text: At dusk, the lamplighter lights the gas lamps, one by one.

scenes.title: Then vs Now
scenes.text: Could you live one day in 1900?

scenes.title: Then vs Now
scenes.text: Then versus now. Before cheap alarm clocks, people paid someone to wake them up.

scenes.title: The knocker-up
scenes.text: In the mill towns of Britain and Ireland, they were called knocker-ups.

scenes.title: Tap, tap, tap
scenes.text: Before dawn, they tapped on bedroom windows with long poles, until you answered.

scenes.title: Or a pea shooter
scenes.text: In London's East End, Mary Smith used a pea shooter, for sixpence a week.

scenes.title: Not just Britain
scenes.text: The Netherlands had them too. There, they were called porders.

scenes.title: Who woke the knocker-up?
scenes.text: So who woke the knocker-up? Usually, nobody. Many worked all night and slept by day.

scenes.title: Then vs Now
scenes.text: Then, a tap on the glass. Now, your phone.
